Introduction: Why Carbonization Happens in Laser Processing

Anyone who has engraved wood or leather has experienced the frustration of dark burn marks, smoky edges, or heavy carbonization. These issues occur when excessive heat builds up—the material absorbs too much laser energy and burns instead of vaporizing cleanly.

To minimize carbonization, operators must understand the relationship between power, speed, frequency, and air assist. These parameters determine whether you’re cutting “hot,” or achieving what professionals call cold working.

Cold working refers to using laser parameters to remove material through rapid vaporization while keeping the surrounding area cool, clean, and unburned.

 

The Science Behind Carbonization

When a laser beam strikes a surface, its photons deliver concentrated energy that excites and breaks molecular bonds. Ideally, the material vaporizes instantly.
However, when energy density is too high—or exposure time is too long—heat diffuses outward, causing oxidation, charring, and carbonized edges.

Key scientific factors that influence carbonization include:

Wavelength
CO₂ lasers (10.6 μm) strongly interact with organic materials such as wood, leather, and paper, making them more prone to overheating.

Pulse Duration
Shorter pulses reduce heat diffusion and allow cooler, cleaner processing.

Thermal Conductivity
Metals dissipate heat quickly, while wood and plastics hold heat, increasing the risk of burning and discoloration.

 

 

What Is “Cold Working” in Laser Processing?

In laser machining, cold working means controlling energy delivery precisely enough that material is removed by instantaneous vaporization instead of prolonged heating.

This does not require cooling the material—it only requires thoughtful parameter tuning.

A properly executed cold-working process provides:

Cleaner edges

Minimal discoloration

Less post-processing (sanding, cleaning)

Higher dimensional accuracy

 

 

Four Core Parameters That Define “Cold Working”

1. Power (W) — Control the Energy Input

Power determines how much energy reaches the surface per unit time.
Too much power burns edges; too little causes incomplete cuts.

Best practice: Start testing at 60–70% of your laser’s rated power, then increase gradually only if needed.

Example:
With a 100W CO₂ laser cutting 3mm plywood → Start at 65W and increase in 5W steps.

Tip: Clean optics regularly—dirty lenses scatter the beam and increase localized heating.

 

 

2. Speed (mm/s) — Control Exposure Time

Speed determines how long the beam stays on one spot.

Higher speed → less exposure, less burning, may require slightly higher power

Lower speed → deeper cuts but increased charring

Cold-working principle:
➡ Use the highest speed that still achieves full penetration.

Typical settings

 

3. Frequency (Hz) — Pulse Density and Heat Distribution

In RF CO₂ systems, frequency determines the number of pulses per second.

Low frequency (1–5 kHz) → fewer pulses → lower heat → cleaner, cooler edges

High frequency (10–20 kHz) → smoother edge quality but more heat buildup

Recommended starting frequencies:

Wood: 3 kHz

Acrylic: 15 kHz

Metal marking: 30–50 kHz

 

 

4. Air Assist — The Hidden Cooling System

Air assist is more than a debris blower—it is a critical cooling and anti-oxidation system.

Benefits include:

Removes smoke and prevents soot redeposition

Reduces oxygen around the beam, preventing burning

Cools the cutting zone, reducing carbonization

Improves kerf cleanliness

Guidelines

Use 0.5–1.5 bar of air pressure

Keep the nozzle 1–2mm above the surface

Use clean, dry compressed air or nitrogen for best results

 

 

Parameter Coordination: The Art of Balance

Cold working is not about a single perfect value—it is about how parameters interact.

 

Key principle:
Optimize synergy, not individual numbers.

 

Material-Specific Strategies to Minimize Carbonization

 

 

Additional Techniques to Reduce Heat Damage

Even with perfect settings, small optimizations can further reduce carbonization:

Apply masking tape or transfer film to protect surfaces

Use multi-pass engraving instead of one deep pass

Clean lenses/mirrors frequently for stable energy delivery

Maintain exact focus—0.5mm of defocus increases beam size and carbonization

Use air-assist filtration to prevent smoke redeposition

 

 

Case Study: Achieving Cold Working on Plywood

A signage workshop used a 100W CO₂ laser to cut 5mm birch plywood.

Initial settings:
90% power, 200 mm/s, 10 kHz, low air assist
→ Resulted in heavy carbonization.

Adjusted settings:

Power reduced to 70%

Speed increased to 300 mm/s

Frequency lowered to 4 kHz

Air pressure increased to 1.2 bar

Final results:

✔ 25% faster total workflow

✔ Zero visible carbonization

✔ Sharper engraving details

 

Conclusion: Controlled Power, Clean Edges

To truly minimize carbonization, you must treat the laser as a precision instrument, not just a high-powered light source.
By controlling power, speed, frequency, and air assist, you can achieve cold working—producing edges that are bright, clean, and dimensionally accurate.

Cold working isn’t magic.
It’s physics, precision, and balance.
